lead: A group is a set with one operation that combines any two elements to a third, is associative, has an identity, and gives every element an inverse. It exists because many systems — integers under addition, non-zero fractions under multiplication, clock arithmetic, rotations of a square — obey the same four rules. Once the rules are proved, one theorem works for all of them. Groups model error-correcting codes, cryptography, symmetry in chemistry and physics, and state machines in software. A subgroup is a smaller group sitting inside a group under the same operation.
prereq: You need: 4.1 Semigroups and monoids for closure, associativity and identity, and Unit 2, Sets, Relations and Functions for subsets and set notation.

blocks.text: A group (G, ∗) is a set G with a binary operation ∗: G×G→G. Compared with a monoid from 4.1, a group adds one demand: every element has an inverse. Four axioms hold. Closure: a,b∈G implies a∗b∈G. Associativity: (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c). Identity: an element e∈G satisfies e∗a = a∗e = a. Inverse: each a∈G has a⁻¹∈G with a∗a⁻¹ = a⁻¹∗a = e.

The order of G, written |G|, is the number of elements. G is abelian if a∗b = b∗a for all a,b∈G. The pair (G,∗) names the set and the operation; a set may be a group under one operation and not another.

items: (Z, +): integers under addition; identity 0; inverse of n is −n; infinite; abelian.
(Q, +): fractions under addition; identity 0; inverse of p/q is −p/q; infinite; abelian.
(Q\{0}, ×): non-zero fractions under multiplication; identity 1; inverse of p/q is q/p; zero is removed because 0 has no multiplicative inverse.
Zₙ under addition modulo n: residues {0,1,…,n−1}; identity 0; inverse of a is −a mod n; |Zₙ|=n; abelian. For n=8, G=Z₈={0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}.
Symmetry groups: rotations of a square form a group of order 4; all eight rotations and reflections form the dihedral group of order 8. The operation is composition of motions.

blocks.text: A subgroup H of (G,∗) is a nonempty subset H⊆G that is itself a group under the same operation ∗. Its identity must be the identity e of G; its inverses are the inverses in G. Every group has the trivial subgroup {e} and the improper subgroup G. A proper subgroup is any subgroup other than G. Some syllabi write 'sub-group'.

items: Two-step test. H is nonempty. Closure: for all a,b∈H, a∗b∈H. Inverse: for all a∈H, a⁻¹∈H. Associativity is inherited from G, and the identity appears because a∗a⁻¹=e for any a∈H.
One-step test. H is nonempty. For all a,b∈H, a∗b⁻¹∈H. Put b=a to get e; put a=e to get b⁻¹; then a∗b∈H follows.

blocks.text: If H and K are subgroups of G, then H∩K is a subgroup. It contains e, so it is nonempty. If a,b∈H∩K, then a,b∈H and a,b∈K; closure in H and K gives a∗b∈H∩K; inverse in H and K gives a⁻¹∈H∩K. This uses the two-step test.

Associativity is never checked inside H. For a,b,c∈H, the equation (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c) is already true in G, and H uses the same operation. Closure keeps a∗b inside H, so the inherited equation stays inside H.
The identity is forced by nonemptiness plus inverse. Pick any a∈H. The inverse condition gives a⁻¹∈H, and closure gives a∗a⁻¹=e∈H. For every h∈H, e∗h=h∗e=h, so e is the identity of H.
The one-step test a∗b⁻¹∈H packs closure and inverse into one condition. Nonemptiness is still required; the empty set would pass the condition vacuously.

figure.caption: H={0,4} sits inside G=Z₈; adding 4 to 4 gives 0, so 4 is its own inverse.

spec.aria: The group G=Z8 under addition contains the subset H={0,4}, which is closed and contains inverses.

examples.question: Let G = Z₈ = {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7} under addition modulo 8. Show that H = {0,4} is a subgroup. List every subgroup of G. State |G|, |H| and the number of subgroups.
steps: The operation is addition modulo 8: a+b is reduced by subtracting 8 when the sum is at least 8.
Nonempty: H has two elements, 0 and 4.
Closure: compute all four sums. 0+0=0, 0+4=4, 4+0=4, 4+4=8≡0 (mod 8). Each result is in H.
Inverses: −0=0∈H. −4≡8−4=4 (mod 8)∈H. Every element has its inverse in H.
Associativity is inherited from Z₈. H is a subgroup. |G|=8 and |H|=2.

Subgroups: {0} of order 1, {0,4} of order 2, {0,2,4,6} of order 4, and G=Z₈ of order 8. These are all: any subgroup containing 1,3,5 or 7 is G; containing 2 but not 1 gives even residues; containing 4 gives {0,4}; otherwise {0}.
examples.answer: H={0,4} is a subgroup of G=Z₈; |G|=8, |H|=2, and G has 4 subgroups: {0}, {0,4}, {0,2,4,6}, Z₈.

traps: Checking closure alone. In (Z,+), the non-negative integers are closed and contain 0, but 1 has no inverse, so they are not a subgroup.
Using a different identity. The identity of H must be the identity e of G, not a new element invented for H.
Forgetting nonemptiness. The empty set satisfies closure and inverse conditions vacuously but is not a subgroup.
Mixing operations. A subset may be a group under a different operation; a subgroup must use the same operation as G.
Assuming a union of subgroups is a subgroup. Closure can fail; H∪K is not automatically a subgroup. The intersection H∩K always is.

quiz.q: State the four group axioms for (G,∗).
quiz.a: Closure: a,b∈G implies a∗b∈G. Associativity: (a∗b)∗c=a∗(b∗c). Identity: there is e∈G with e∗a=a∗e=a. Inverse: each a∈G has a⁻¹∈G with a∗a⁻¹=a⁻¹∗a=e.

quiz.q: Why is (Q,×) not a group, while (Q\{0},×) is a group?
quiz.a: In (Q,×), the element 0 has no multiplicative inverse, so the inverse axiom fails. Removing 0 leaves every non-zero fraction p/q with inverse q/p, identity 1, closure and associativity, so (Q\{0},×) is a group.

quiz.q: In G=Z₁₀ under addition modulo 10, is H={0,5} a subgroup? Check closure, identity and inverses.
quiz.a: Yes. Closure: 5+5=10≡0 (mod 10), and sums with 0 stay in H. Identity: 0∈H. Inverses: −0=0 and −5≡5 (mod 10). So H is a subgroup of order 2.

quiz.q: List all subgroups of Z₆ under addition modulo 6.
Let H and K be subgroups of a group G. Prove that H∩K is a subgroup using the two-step test.
quiz.a: e∈H and e∈K, so e∈H∩K and H∩K is nonempty. Let a,b∈H∩K. Then a,b∈H and a,b∈K. Closure in H gives a∗b∈H; closure in K gives a∗b∈K; hence a∗b∈H∩K. Inverse in H gives a⁻¹∈H; inverse in K gives a⁻¹∈K; hence a⁻¹∈H∩K. By the two-step test, H∩K is a subgroup.

quiz.q: Give a subset of (Z,+) that is closed under addition and contains 0 but is not a subgroup. Explain which axiom fails.
quiz.a: The set N₀={0,1,2,…} is closed under addition and contains 0. It is not a subgroup because 1 has no inverse in N₀; −1 is not in the set. The inverse axiom fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Groups appear in public-key cryptography through elliptic curves, where points on a curve form a group under a geometric addition rule. They also appear in error-correcting codes, molecular symmetry, and reversible state machines. Search next for 'elliptic curve group law' and 'group actions'. A subgroup test is the first tool for checking whether a smaller set preserves the same structure.
